answer.answer: To update your Social Security card after a legal name change due to marriage, you need to tell Social Security so you can get a corrected card, and if you are working, also tell your employer. The evidence of the legal name change can include a marriage document, divorce decree, certificate of naturalization showing the new name, or a court order approving the name change. Documents must be current and not expired; photocopies, notarized copies, and receipts showing you applied for a document are not accepted. If the name-change document does not give enough information to identify you in SSA records, or if you changed your name more than two years ago, you must show an identity document in your prior name as shown in SSA records (an expired identity document in your old name is acceptable); if you lack one, SSA may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name if your identity can be properly established. For your New York driver's license, bring to a DMV office a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44), your current license (or at least 6 points of proof of identity), and the original or certified copy of your U.S. marriage certificate (or U.S. divorce documents or other court papers for a name change issued in the U.S.). You must also update your photo when you change your name on your license. In addition, if the name on your license application does not match the name on your identity, lawful status, and Social Security proofs, you must bring court or government-issued proof documenting the event causing the name change, such as a marriage license, divorce decree, adoption, or court order document. The DMV process also requires a new photo.

answer.answer: To update your Social Security card after a legal name change due to marriage, you need to tell Social Security so you can get a corrected card; if you are working, also tell your employer. You must provide evidence of the legal name change, such as a marriage document, divorce decree, certificate of naturalization showing the new name, or court order approving the name change. If the name-change document does not give enough information to identify you in SSA records, or if you changed your name more than two years ago (four years if under 18), you must show an identity document in your prior name as shown in SSA records; an expired identity document in your old name is acceptable. If you lack an identity document in your prior name, SSA may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name if your identity can be properly established. Documents must be current and not expired, and SSA cannot accept photocopies, notarized copies, or receipts showing you applied for a document. One document may serve two purposes (for example, a U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity).

To update your New York driver's license after a legal name change, bring to a DMV office: a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44); your current license, permit, or non-driver ID (or at least 6 points of proof of identity); and the original or a certified copy of your U.S. marriage certificate (or U.S. divorce documents or other court papers for a name change issued in the U.S.). You must also update your photo when you change your name on your license. Note that if the name on your application does not match your identity, lawful status, and Social Security proofs, you must bring court- or government-issued proof documenting the name change, such as a marriage license.

For your Social Security card: because you legally changed your name due to marriage, you need to tell Social Security so you can get a corrected card; if you are working, also tell your employer. Failing to report the change may prevent your wages from being posted correctly to your Social Security record (which may lower future benefits) and may cause delays when you file your taxes. You must provide evidence of the legal name change, such as a marriage document, divorce decree, certificate of naturalization showing the new name, or court order approving the name change. If the name-change document does not give SSA enough information to identify you in its records, or if you changed your name more than two years ago (four years if under 18), you must show an identity document in your prior name as shown in SSA records; an expired identity document in your old name is acceptable. If you lack an identity document in your prior name, SSA may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name if your identity can be properly established. SSA cannot accept photocopies or notarized copies, or a receipt showing you applied for a document, and all documents must be current and not expired. One document may serve two purposes (for example, a U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity).

For your New York driver's license: bring to a DMV office a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44); your current license, permit, or non-driver ID (or at least 6 points of proof of identity); and the original or a certified copy of your U.S. marriage certificate (or U.S. divorce documents or other court papers for a name change issued in the U.S.). When you change your name on your license, you must update your photo. Also, if the name on your license application does not match the name on your identity, lawful status, and Social Security proofs, you must bring court- or government-issued proof documenting the event causing your name change, such as a marriage license.

answer.answer: To apply for GI Bill education benefits, first check whether you're eligible for VA education benefits, gather the documents and information you'll need, and see what benefits you'll get at the school you want to attend using the GI Bill Comparison Tool. The documents and information needed to apply include your Social Security number, bank account direct deposit information, your education and military history, and basic information about the school or training facility you want to attend or are attending now. You can also apply by mail (call 888-GI-BILL-1, 888-442-4551, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ET, to request that the application be sent to you, then fill it out and mail it to the VA regional claims processing office in the same location as your school), in person at a VA regional benefit office, by working with your school's certifying official (usually in the Registrar or Financial Aid office), or with the help of a trained professional called an accredited representative. Note that if you're applying for Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (Chapter 31) or educational and career counseling (Chapter 36) benefits, you'll need to use a different application. The evidence provided does not include information on how to apply for federal student aid.

For a lost DD214, it indicates that if you don't have a copy of the necessary form, you can request it by submitting a Standard Form 180, Request Pertaining to Military Records, from the National Archives, and you can find out how to request military service records online, by mail, or by fax.

To add veteran status to your New York driver's license, you must provide proof of an honorable discharge, such as a U.S. Department of Defense Form DD-214 that indicates an honorable discharge (or a DD-215 if discharged before January 1, 1950, or an Honorable Discharge form WD AGO 5). There is no additional fee for the veteran status designation, but all regular transaction fees apply. Once you receive the veteran designation, it will automatically appear on all your future DMV documents when you replace or renew. You can apply by mail by sending a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44), your proof of honorable discharge (photocopies), and your original documents to DMV License Production Bureau, Room 331, 6 Empire State Plaza, Albany, NY 12228. You cannot apply by phone or online. If you have a Standard license and want to change to a REAL ID or Enhanced while adding veteran status, you must come into a DMV office and bring your proof of honorable discharge (original or photocopies). The evidence does not explain how to obtain a replacement copy of a lost DD214.

You can address both parts separately, but the evidence does not cover every step.

Getting another copy of your lost DD214: The VA evidence says that if you don't have a copy of the necessary form, you can request it by submitting a Standard Form 180, Request Pertaining to Military Records, from the National Archives, and you can find out how to request military service records online, by mail, or by fax. (This guidance appears in a VA CHAMPVA benefits document, so it is not specific to New York DMV procedures.)

Adding veteran status to your New York driver's license: As a qualified U.S. military veteran who was honorably discharged with a NY State driver license, you can have the word "Veteran" printed on the upper left-hand of your photo document. There is no additional fee for the veteran status designation, but all regular transaction fees apply. After you receive the veteran designation, it will automatically be on all your future DMV documents when you replace or renew.

To apply, you must provide proof of an honorable discharge. Acceptable proofs are a U.S. Department of Defense Form DD-214 that indicates an honorable discharge, a form DD-215 if discharged before January 1, 1950, or an Honorable Discharge form WD AGO 5.

By mail: Send a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44), your proof of honorable discharge (send photocopies), and your original documents to DMV License Production Bureau, Room 331, 6 Empire State Plaza, Albany, NY 12228. You cannot apply by phone or online.

At a DMV office: If you have a Standard license and want to change to a REAL ID or Enhanced while adding your veteran status, you must come into a DMV office. You will also need to bring your proof of honorable discharge (original or photocopies).

Note: The DMV evidence does not explain how to obtain a replacement copy of a lost DD214, and the VA evidence does not explain how to add veteran status to a New York driver's license. No cross-agency rule should be inferred beyond what each source states.

answer.answer:
For VA disability compensation: VA disability compensation is a monthly tax-free payment to Veterans who got sick or injured while serving in the military, or whose service made an existing condition worse. You may qualify for benefits for physical conditions such as a chronic illness or injury. Eligibility generally requires that you served on active duty, active duty for training, or inactive duty training, and that you have a disability rating for your service-connected condition (plus at least one additional listed requirement). So a leg injury incurred during military service that causes major difficulty walking could potentially support a claim, subject to meeting these eligibility criteria.

For a New York disabled parking permit: New York requires proof of disability when applying for a parking permit or plates. If you have an obvious, visible, permanent disability—such as complete or partial loss of a leg or foot—the medical statement requirement may be waived by the local issuing agent for a permit (or by a DMV supervisor for plates). If you moved to New York, you must still provide the required proof of disability even if you had parking privileges elsewhere, and an out-of-state permit cannot be exchanged for a NYS permit or plates. Check with your local issuing agent before applying.

The evidence does not specify the full list of qualifying disabilities for a New York parking permit or the complete application procedure, so those details would need to be confirmed with the local issuing agent.

answer.answer: The evidence explains how to exchange a current New York State driver license for a non-driver ID card, but it does not explain how to apply for Social Security disability benefits. To exchange the license, you can apply by mail or in a DMV office. At an office, complete an Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44), then bring your current license, your application, and payment. By mail, send a completed MV-44, your current license (or one expired for less than two years), a photocopy of proof of Supplemental Security Income if required, and payment; do not mail your original document. If you want a reduced or no-fee replacement, you must apply by mail or at a DMV office (not online) and provide proof of SSI eligibility, such as a Notice of Award, COLA letter, notice of change in payment, SSA-L8151 Third Party Query letter, or SSA-2258 Benefit Verification letter; for the Benefit Verification letter you must call the Social Security Administration in advance at 1-800-772-1213. Because the evidence does not cover applying for Social Security disability benefits, that part of the question cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

You can apply online, or by calling 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday; representatives can make an appointment for your application to be taken over the telephone or at a convenient Social Security office. Note that Social Security disability benefits will not begin until the sixth full month of disability. To switch your current New York driver's license to a non-driver ID card, you can exchange a NY State driver license that is current (or expired within the last 2 years) for a NY State non-driver ID card; you must apply by mail or in a DMV office. As a Veteran, submit a Request for Change of Program or Place of Training (VA Form 22-1995), which you can complete online. How do I show that I qualify for a TPD discharge?

answer.answer: Based on the evidence, you may be eligible for VA Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E) benefits if you are a Veteran who did not receive a dishonorable discharge, have a service-connected disability rating of at least 10% from VA, and apply for VR&E services. Since your rating is 20%, you meet the 10% threshold. VR&E programs can help you learn new skills, find a new job, start a new business, get educational counseling, or return to your former job, and eligibility is tied to having a service-connected disability that limits your ability to work or prevents you from working. Note that your basic period of eligibility generally ends 12 years from the date you received notice of your separation from active military service or your first VA service-connected disability rating, though it may be extended if a Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor finds you have a serious employment handicap. answer.answer: For a VA Veterans Pension, eligibility depends on several factors: you must have served on active duty for at least 24 months and meet at least one of these conditions—being at least 65 years old, having a permanent and total disability, being a patient in a nursing home for long-term care because of a disability, or getting Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income. You must also have served during an eligible wartime period (such as the Mexican Border period, World War I, World War II, the Korean conflict, or the Vietnam War era), must not have received a dishonorable discharge, and your yearly family income and net worth must meet limits set by Congress (net worth includes your spouse's net worth and all personal property except your house, car, and most home furnishings, minus debts). For Social Security retirement benefits, you can start your retirement benefit at any point from age 62 up until age 70, with the amount higher the longer you delay; applying before full retirement age reduces your benefit, while delaying past full retirement age up to age 70 increases it through Delayed Retirement Credits. If you are within three months of age 65 or older and not ready to start monthly Social Security benefits, you can use the online retirement application to sign up just for Medicare and apply for retirement benefits later.

answer.answer: To qualify for a VA Veterans Pension, you must meet both of these requirements: you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, and your yearly family income and net worth meet certain limits set by Congress (your net worth includes all personal property you own except your house, your car, and most home furnishings, minus any debt you owe, and includes your spouse's net worth). In addition, you must have served on active duty for at least 24 months and meet at least one of these: you are at least 65 years old, have a permanent and total disability, are a patient in a nursing home for long-term care because of a disability, or are getting Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income. You must also have served during an eligible wartime period recognized under current law.

The evidence provided does not address VA Veterans Pension eligibility; it only covers Social Security retirement benefits. For the Social Security part: you can start your retirement benefit at any point from age 62 up until age 70, and your benefit amount will be higher the longer you delay starting it. If you are within three months of age 65 or older and not ready to start your monthly Social Security benefits yet, you can use the online retirement application to sign up just for Medicare and wait to apply for your retirement or spouse's benefits later. Applying before full retirement age reduces your benefits, while delaying past full retirement age up to age 70 increases them through Delayed Retirement Credits.

VA Veterans Pension: Based on the VA evidence, eligibility requires meeting both of these: you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, and your yearly family income and net worth meet certain limits set by Congress (net worth includes all personal property you own except your house, your car, and most home furnishings, minus any debt you owe, and includes your spouse's net worth). You must also have served on active duty for at least 24 months and meet at least one of these: you are at least 65 years old, have a permanent and total disability, are a patient in a nursing home for long-term care because of a disability, or are getting Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income. You must also have served during an eligible wartime period recognized under current law. Social Security retirement benefits: You can start your retirement benefit at any point from age 62 up until age 70, and your benefit amount will be higher the longer you delay starting it (this adjustment is usually permanent). Applying before full retirement age reduces your benefits; delaying past full retirement age up to age 70 can increase them through Delayed Retirement Credits. Separately, if you are within three months of age 65 or older and not ready to start your monthly Social Security benefits yet, you can use the online retirement application to sign up just for Medicare and wait to apply for your retirement or spouse's benefits later. Note: the VA and Social Security rules above come from separate agencies' materials and are presented independently; the evidence does not establish any cross-agency interaction between them.

You'll need your bank's routing number and account number. You can also change your information by mail using VA Form 24-0296, or by phone at 800-827-1000 (Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. ET), or by visiting your nearest VA regional office.

To change the direct deposit for your Social Security retirement benefits, you can start or change Direct Deposit online (for Social Security benefits only), contact your bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, or call Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). To do it online, log in to your my Social Security account, select the blue Benefits & Payment Details link on the right side of the screen, scroll down and select the Update Direct Deposit button, choose whether you are the owner or co-owner of the bank account, enter your bank account information and select Next, then review and verify your banking information and select Submit, then Done. You can also decide when your change will take effect using the My Profile tab within my Social Security. You will need your Social Security number, bank routing transit number, account type (checking or savings), and account number. If you don't have a my Social Security account, creating a free one takes less than 10 minutes.

You can also change it by mail using VA Form 24-0296, by phone at 800-827-1000 (Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. ET), or by visiting your nearest VA regional office.

Social Security retirement: You can start or change Direct Deposit online (for Social Security benefits only), contact your bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, or call Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). To do it online, log in to your my Social Security account, select the blue Benefits & Payment Details link, scroll down and select Update Direct Deposit, choose whether you are the owner or co-owner of the account, enter your bank account information and select Next, then review and verify and select Submit, then Done. answer.answer: For New York disability parking privileges: if your disability is not permanent, you may qualify for a temporary permit valid for up to six (months); if you have an obvious, visible, permanent disability such as complete or partial loss of a leg or foot, the medical statement requirement may be waived by a DMV supervisor when applying for license plates or by the local issuing agent when applying for a permit. If you already have disability license plates, a locality may accept your registration as proof for issuing a permit, and you should check with your local issuing agent before applying. For federal student loan forbearance: you can submit a request to your student loan servicer, often using a form, and for some types of forbearance you must provide documentation showing you meet the eligibility requirements. A general (discretionary) forbearance can be requested if you are temporarily unable to make scheduled monthly payments due to financial difficulties or medical expenses, and your servicer decides whether to grant it. Note that interest accrues during forbearance and, if unpaid, will capitalize (be added to your principal balance).
